sentences.text: Revenue, net interest income plus noninterest income, rose from $96.6 billion in FY2016 to $182 billion in FY2025 [D5][D206], a 7.3% CAGR.
The path was a step change, not a smooth compound: revenue grew 22.9% in FY2023 and 12.3% in FY2024 after a 5.8% gain in FY2022 [D179][D202][D154].
The FY2023 jump came from higher rates lifting net interest income, which rose 33.8% that year [D174], with deposit margin expansion on higher rates cited across segments [P37][P50].
Growth then stalled to 2.8% in FY2025 [D226], as net interest income rose only 3.1% [D221] and noninterest income 2.4% [D222].
North America remains the core at 76.6% of revenue in FY2025 [D249], but contributed only 0.2pp of growth that year [D251].
International was the FY2025 driver: EMEA added 1.2pp and Asia-Pacific 1.2pp [D276][D301], with Asia-Pacific revenue up 17.3% [D300].
Firmwide, net interest income growth was driven by higher Markets net interest income and higher revolving balances in Card Services, largely offset by deposit margin compression [P28].
Profit grew slower than revenue in FY2025: net income fell 2.6% [D214] while revenue rose 2.8% [D226], and noninterest expense grew 4.2% [D225].
Per-share growth outran net income over the window, with diluted EPS compounding at 13.9% [F115] against net income at 9.7% [F113], as the diluted share count fell 3.4% in FY2025 [D224].
The efficiency ratio was 52.4% in FY2025 [D207], better than the 57.2% window median [D333] and near the 51.7% window low of FY2024 [D331].
That is well below the banks peer median of 61.7% [D337], placing JPM at the 0th percentile of the seven-bank group [D336].
Noninterest expense rose 4% in FY2025 on higher compensation, brokerage and distribution fees, auto lease depreciation, and technology and marketing investment [P26].
The credit-loss provision rose to 7.8% of revenue in FY2025 [D208] from 6.0% in FY2024 [D185], above the 6.0% peer median [D341].
The higher provision reflected net increases in loan and commitment portfolios, credit-quality changes, updated leveraged-loan loss assumptions, and estimated fraud losses [P15].
Operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure for a bank; capital return is the better lens.
Operating cash flow was negative $148 billion in FY2025 [F60], or -2.59x net income [D204], against $57.0 billion of net income [F30].
The outflow resulted from higher trading assets, higher securities borrowed, net loan originations, and higher other assets, partly offset by net income [P21].
Buybacks plus dividends of $48.2 billion in FY2025 [D205] were 0.85x net income of $57.0 billion [F30], funded from a deep liquidity base rather than operating cash.
Return on average equity was 16.1% in FY2025 [D213], against a banks peer median of 11.8% [D339], ranking at the 100th percentile of seven peers [D338].
Loans were 57.3% of deposits in FY2025 [D211], up from 43.1% in FY2021 [D115], as loans grew to $1.47 trillion [X197] on higher CIB Markets and AWM securities-based lending [P4].
Available borrowing capacity at the FHLBs and Federal Reserve discount window was about $449 billion at year-end FY2025 [P9].
Capital return was $48.2 billion in FY2025 [D205], including $31.6 billion of buybacks [X102] and $16.6 billion of dividends [X112], cutting the diluted share count 3.4% [D224].

Net income for FY2021 through FY2025 in the metrics table comes from the proxy pay-versus-performance table, not the 10-K, differing by up to 0.10% [R1]; the 10-K figure for FY2025 is $57.0 billion [X20].
The provision rose to $14.2 billion in FY2025 [X147] from $10.7 billion in FY2024 [X146], lifting it to 7.8% of revenue [D208] and the 75th percentile of four peers [D340].
Criticized wholesale exposure rose to $48.5 billion from $44.7 billion, driven by SPEs, Consumer & Retail, Banks & Finance Companies, Healthcare, and Chemicals & Plastics [P2].
The allowance for credit losses rose to $25.8 billion [X216], or 1.8% of loans [D212], leaving limited cushion if credit deteriorates further.
Watch the efficiency ratio: a move above the 57.2% window median [D333] would reverse the FY2024-FY2025 improvement, reported in the FY2026 10-K.
Watch the credit-loss provision as a share of revenue: a rise above the FY2025 level of 7.8% [D208] would confirm the deteriorating credit trend flagged by criticized exposure [P2].

Watch net interest income growth: a return above the FY2023 pace of 33.8% [D174] would signal the rate-driven step change is resuming, while a fall below the FY2025 3.1% [D221] would confirm the stall.
